newsitem.title: USA: UPS opens door to compromise with Teamsters.
newsitem.headline: UPS opens door to compromise with Teamsters.

text.p: United Parcel Service and Teamsters officials met on Thursday to try to settle the nation's biggest strike in 27 years as UPS Chairman James Kelly said his company might soften its previous unbending stance.

Kelly had declared the dispute at an impasse on Wednesday but in an interview on Thursday he struck a more conciliatory tone on pensions and whether UPS's "final" offer was open to change under the right conditions.

"We think the pension issue is very important for both our people and the future of our company, but as I said there is no one or two single issues that will determine whether we're able to reach agreement," he told wire service reporters in a telephone interview from Atlanta.
The UPS chief made his comments as the cost of the strike climbed toward a half-billion dollars and a new public opinion poll showed a majority of the public backing the union.
Kelly also said that if progress came out of Thursday's talks, which were billed as informal, that may lead UPS eventually to drop what it has called its "last, best and final" offer.
"If those informal discussions lead us to believe that the negotiations could be concluded at some point in time, then the last, best and final offer would cease to exist," he said.

In addition to a dispute over adding more full-time jobs, UPS has insisted on establishing a new pension fund -- which would cover only UPS workers -- to replace the existing fund covering Teamster workers at dozens of companies, mostly trucking lines.
Richard Hurd, professor of labor studies at Cornell University, found Kelly's comments encouraging.

"It's the first sign of any flexibility from the company since they first made their 'last, best and final' offer," he said. "It's not a guarantee that something will happen, but it means there's a possibility."
But a Teamster spokesman was cautious.
"There's no real reason to jump up and down until we see what happens," said Steve Trossman.
As the informal talks continued, CNN released a new poll showing solid support for the striking UPS drivers -- the second poll this week with that finding.
CNN found 55 percent of those polled support the union, while 27 percent support the company position.

Its survey of 819 adults, conducted Aug. 12 and 13 with an error rate of 3 percentage points, found that 75 percent oppose intervention by U.S. President Bill Clinton in the strike, as does the union. Only 21 percent want him to intervene, as does UPS.
The strike has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company and sent thousands of businesses scrambling to find other ways to ship their goods.

The U.S. Postal Service estimated on Thursday that it is receiving 15 percent to 20 percent of the 12 million daily package business of UPS, and has hired more than 4,000 temporary workers to cope with the added business volume.

Kelly's comments on Thursday seemed to improve chances for a pact to end the strike by 185,000 sorters, loaders and drivers, now in its 11th day, which UPS says is costing it $300 million a week. The company is shipping about 10 percent of its normal daily volume.

While Kelly was talking with reporters, federal mediator John Calhoun Wells was meeting in a Washington hotel with Teamster President Ron Carey and UPS negotiator Dave Murray, who met face to face for the first time since Saturday.

Labor Secretary Alexis Herman was nearby in case her help was needed, a Labor Department spokesman said. But Herman -- who persuaded the parties to return to the table -- did not directly involve herself in the talks.
Clinton has decided not to intervene in the strike, the largest since the postal workers' strike of 1970, but the administration is closely watching its effects.

UPS has repeatedly urged presidential intervention and won the backing on Thursday of the American Small Businesses Association, which urged Clinton in a letter to play "a more direct, assertive role" in ending the strike.

The two sides had hardened their positions on Tuesday, when the AFL-CIO labor group said it would provide loans to cover the $10 million in weekly pay for striking workers while UPS warned it would cut 15,000 jobs due to lost business.
In a related action, UPS sued its pilots in a state court in Louisville, Ky., accusing them of intimidating pilots of independently chartered planes into not carrying its packages.

The company said it was seeking a temporary restraining order on Thursday night to prevent the 2,000-member Independent Pilots Association, the UPS pilots' union, from intimidating charter pilots at its half-dozen U.S. hubs.
IPA members are already refusing to cross Teamsters picket lines, grounding UPS planes.
The head of that union, Robert Miller, told a news conference earlier Thursday that the pilots might strike near Christmas in an unrelated pay dispute.
About 2,000 IPA members normally fly UPS's fleet of 500 planes. They have been working without a contract since December 1995.
